slides.heading: The History of Halloween
slides.body: From ancient Celtic fire festivals to the world's most beloved spooky celebration

slides.heading: Ancient Celtic Origins
slides.body: Halloween began as Samhain, a Celtic harvest festival marking the end of summer. Celts believed the boundary between the living and the dead dissolved on October 31st, allowing spirits to roam the earth.

slides.heading: Bonfires and Costumes
slides.body: Celts lit massive bonfires to ward off evil spirits and donned animal hides as disguises. Druids used the occasion to make prophecies about the winter ahead — a time of great uncertainty and danger.

slides.heading: Roman Influence
slides.body: When Rome conquered Celtic lands, Samhain merged with two Roman festivals: Feralia (honoring the dead) and a day celebrating Pomona, goddess of fruit and trees. This is why we bob for apples to this day.

slides.heading: The Christian Transformation
slides.body: In 609 AD, the Catholic Church established All Saints' Day on November 1st. The evening before became 'All Hallows' Eve,' eventually shortened to Halloween. Church feasts absorbed many pagan traditions.

slides.heading: Jack-o'-Lanterns
slides.body: Irish legend tells of 'Stingy Jack,' a trickster who bargained with the Devil and was condemned to wander the earth with only a carved turnip for light. Irish immigrants brought this tradition to America, where pumpkins proved far easier to carve.

slides.heading: Trick-or-Treating
slides.body: Medieval 'souling' had the poor visiting homes for food in exchange for prayers for the dead. In America during the 1920s–1950s, trick-or-treating emerged as a community-wide custom to reduce Halloween mischief and bring neighborhoods together.

slides.heading: Halloween Goes Global
slides.body: What began as a Celtic tradition spread through the British Isles and then exploded across North America. Today, Halloween is celebrated in over 30 countries and generates more than $10 billion in spending in the US alone annually.

slides.heading: Modern Halloween
slides.body: From haunted houses and horror movies to elaborate costumes and themed parties, Halloween has evolved into a month-long cultural phenomenon. It is now the second-largest commercial holiday in the United States after Christmas.

slides.heading: Happy Halloween!
slides.body: Over 2,000 years of history — and every October 31st, the ancient tradition of embracing the mysterious, the spooky, and the unknown lives on. May your night be filled with more treats than tricks!
